By applying our method to a sample of annotated EMEQ-1.7 data, we've demonstrated noticeable improvements in a subsequent machine learning classification task. In comparison with a straightforward re-annotation method, our approach yields a 12% increase in accuracy. Additionally, we've found that our method is effective in integrating user feedback into annotated data, which can be utilized as input for machine learning models.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, they need to be able to construct mental maps of their environment based on the data they collect through sensors. The maps they create should accurately reflect the environment's layout and pose, facilitating effective path-planning and obstacle avoidance. Unlike static maps, these maps evolve with each new sensor reading, changing in response to new data or lost localization. Our new mapping algorithm, HiTMap, is a robust and efficient way for robots to build maps of their surroundings without relying on prior knowledge of the environment. HiTMap generates detailed maps of the space by tracking the layout and positioning of landmarks, and includes innovative navigation features such as localized landmark addition/deletion and moving objects detection. Our results show that HiTMap offers significant improvements in mapping accuracy and efficiency, and enables safe and efficient navigation through complex, dynamic environments.

One of the most sensitive methods for determining changes in a local magnetic field is through atomic interferometry. While this approach can be very sensitive to acceleration and temperature fluctuations, there's a way to make it even more sensitive to magnetic field changes by positioning atomic beams near superconducting materials that exhibit the Meissner effect. Since atomic interferometry is sensitive to the slight deflections of atomic beams caused by the formation of magnetic vortices in the superconductors, this effect could be used to detect very small changes in a local magnetic field, particularly spatial variations. This approach has the potential to compete with the most sensitive methods for detecting magnetic field changes and could be particularly useful in a variety of environments, both terrestrial and aerospace.

This study explores a type of finite mixture models where the probability distribution belongs to a given set of probability measures on a given space, and it incorporates an approach from stochastic geometry and Choquet theory. A distinctive feature of these models is the use of a convex structure to define the distribution, which is made possible by the assumption that the mixture has a finite number of components. A key aspect examined in this research involves the convex hull of the mixture distributions, as well as its relationship to the convex hull of the component distributions. A major contribution of this work is the derivation of an explicit formula for the convex hull of the mixture distributions, which can be used to extend existing results from the literature. Additionally, this research provides two distinct applications of the obtained formula, one related to the aggregation of stochastic models and the other related to the estimation of mixture models.

Due to the complex nature of memory management, developers rarely work directly with memory on GPUs, instead utilizing object-based programming models that abstract this process. Although this convenience comes with a cost, as memory allocation becomes slower and less efficient. Current solutions focus on accelerating memory allocation through parallelization, but neglect optimization of memory access for real-world applications. In contrast, our proposed DynaSOAr allocator targets object-based programming on GPUs and prioritizes both parallel memory allocation and optimal memory placement for reduced coalescing losses. We test DynaSOAr against existing allocators and alternative optimization techniques, demonstrating its superiority in applications prone to cache misses. Furthermore, our framework provides a versatile platform for researchers to explore various memory access optimizations.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn clusters on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a large Mn cluster, the YSR state's formation was examined as it interacted with the Mn cluster's boundary layers. Conversely, when a large amount of sulfur was incorporated into the cluster, the YSR state disappeared due to spin polarization of the Nb atoms and subsequent formation of sulfur-Nb bonds. As a result, the YSR state's behavior was found to be highly sensitive to both the bulk and surface properties of the material, demonstrating the complexity of which which cannot be simplified by a single parameter.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years based on spectral characteristics and rotational velocity. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. A fourth smaller planet with an orbital period of $84.839$ days was also identified, and it's suspected to be an Earth-sized planet. Evaluating the irradiation levels suggests that the innermost planet experiences high heat stress, while the most externally located planet cools quickly, and the middle planets may have conditions similar to those of Neptune's moons.

We investigated the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defect states within the rutile TiO2 matrix using a (101) [001] slab model. Our calculations demonstrated that these defects prefer a supercell method with 2x2x1 configuration. Analyzing the band structures and phase space diagrams enabled us to identify the preferred doping orientations for both elements. Notably, we found that nitrogen tends to create a magnetic moment when doped into the TiO2 lattice, a phenomenon not previously observed. Our study further explored the effects of oxygen vacancy incorporation in both nitrogen and carbon doped TiO2, discovering that such vacancies cause the loss of magnetic properties in nitrogen doped materials but induce magnetism in carbon doped materials. Lastly, we examined the surface TiO2 (101) [001] slab and found that both elements exhibit minimal deviation from their bulk behaviors.

The frequent production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider poses a challenge in identifying signatures of new physics that enhance top-quark pair creation, particularly through exclusive production where the collider beam remains undetected.  A novel strategy is proposed to overcome this difficulty by focusing on the elastic production of top-quark pairs in proton-proton collisions, where the colliding protons remain intact after reconstructing the top-quark pair from the collision's other products.  This approach is effective in pinning down the rate of elastic production, thereby providing valuable information about the strong interaction's properties at high energies and offering a straightforward path to discovering new physics that interacts with the top quark through the strong force.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin introduced the concept of upper richness within Ramsey theory, specifically focusing on upper bounded graphs. They established that every infinite graph contains either an isomorphic copy of a specific infinite graph dubbed the ``parent,'' which possesses a particular ordering, or an infinitely vast version of another defined as the ``daughter,'' characterized by a distinct ordering. Here, we refer to the parent as $P_\infty$ and the daughter as $D_\infty$. Our primary objective in this study is to determine the upper rich complexity of $D_\infty$ in relation to $P_\infty$, denoted by $\rho(D_\infty|P_\infty)$. Specifically, we aim to investigate how the upper rich complexity of $D_\infty$ compares to $P_\infty$ across varying scenarios.

Our analysis highlights that noise from qudit manufacturing and coupling has different effects on vacuum entanglement and spontaneous parametric down-conversion entanglement in quantum electrodynamics. Specifically, the rate of qudit loss affects vacuum entanglement exponentially, qudit misphase error influences cross-correlation exponentially, qudit phase error affects cross-correlation linearly, and qudit gain or loss affects the frequency of qudit entanglement generation or destruction. Furthermore, the magnitude of qudit gain or loss impacts qudit entanglement generation rates either exponentially or linearly. Our findings also reveal that qudit entanglement generation is more resistant to noise from qudit dephasing than vacuum entanglement generation. Consequently, our analysis suggests that using qudit systems with N duality levels greater than 2 may result in vacuum entanglement generation instead of sQED, whereas those with N duality levels less than 2 lead to sQED with qudit loss, qudit dephasing, or qudit phase error, respectively. Additionally, our research indicates that noise similar to qudit gain occurs in coupled qudit systems with N duality levels less than 2, leading to qudit entanglement generation without the need for a pump.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the effects of a circularly polarized laser on a thin film target. The results show that, when the intensity of the laser is high enough, the positrons emitted in a specific direction become highly polarized, with values exceeding 90%. In fact, due to the polarization of the electron layer, targets with a specific orientation can exhibit very high polarization levels, potentially reaching 100%. These findings indicate that film targets are capable of producing extremely polarized positrons, with values dependent on the angle and targeted electron layer. The degree of polarization can also be influenced by the thickness of the target, although only minimal impact is exhibited when the thickness exceeds a certain limit. In general, our findings demonstrate that film targets can serve as a highly efficient source of polarized positrons.

Given a finite group G and a subgroup H of G, we examine the structure of H within the group G, focusing on the number of coset types relative to H as our main measure. This count is reflected in the number of G H coset types, which we'll denote by |Nh/G| (here Nh represents the left cosets of H in G). Our investigation leads to a precise characterization of groups for which this coset type count results in a polynomial function. In particular, we show these groups comprise subsets of the symmetric groups Sn, including finite classical groups and some members of the orthogonal groups On.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature detector with a small power supply. The design utilizes two threshold voltages provided by two bulk-embedded PMOS transistors with different well connections. This results in the device having two threshold voltages that vary with temperature, allowing for a two-point calibration to determine the absolute temperature. The design is compact, occupying an area of 0.032$mm^2$, and features a simple architecture with only four access transistors. The proposed temperature detector can operate within a wide temperature range of $-25{\deg}C$ to $150{\deg}C$ and boasts a high resolution of $0.24{\deg}C$ along with an acceptable inaccuracy of $\pm$1.4{\deg}C. The development of this design involved creating a simulation environment that mimicked the behavior of real-world integrated circuit manufacturing processes. The temperature detector was tested in a virtual environment using a 0.18$\mu$m CMOS process and mounted on a microcontroller for actual temperature measurements.

This study focuses on integrating geometric frameworks from symplectic geometry within the context of Lie groupoids and differential stacks. We demonstrate how classical geometric concepts such as Poisson structures, symplectic forms, and Hamiltonian vector fields are defined along a groupoid's orbits by utilizing the natural morphism associated with a Lie groupoid. Furthermore, we examine how these definitions extend to differential stacks by employing the geometric framework associated with a presheaf of Lie groupoids.

A statistical analysis of infrared dark clouds was used to develop a framework for identifying core evolution, specifically the stage preceding massive star formation. By comparing the mass and radius of 19 gas-filled cores within the Dragon infrared dark cloud using radiative transfer modeling, we found that core masses range from 0.2 to 8.6 solar masses and radii range from 0.7 to 2.4 solar radii. Calculating the radial expansion showed that in about half of the cases, cores have radii greater than 1.5 solar radii. Notably, this phenomenon is more prevalent in dense cores with masses above 6 solar masses. Furthermore, a correlation between the spectral line width and the radial expansion rate suggests that core radii may increase with internal pressure, which could be a key factor in massive star formation formation formation.

We develop a one-step recurrence formula to represent Gaussian random fields on the sphere at a single point in time, building on the prior method by Temam for sphere-based fields that evolve dynamically. This achievement is credited to a significant observation made by Basse-O'Connor, Naik, and Sunde, regarding the equivalence of certain second-order difference operators and Laplacian operators on the sphere. By utilizing this connection, we derive an intuitive representation of random fields on the sphere in terms of differential equations, facilitated by the availability of an extensive library of solving tools for these equations. This paper also outlines a similar but more complicated one-step recurrence formula for fields that evolve dynamically.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface properties, especially when they have a high interfacial tension relative to their bulk properties.  Despite the significance of this phenomenon in natural and engineering contexts, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood.  This study delves into the relationship between surface texture and the friction experienced by a liquid, utilizing a rigid plate pushed into a layer of soap foam as a model system.  Our findings reveal that deep textures can substantially increase friction, and that this enhancement stems from the creation of edges and corners where the foam film breaks and new surfaces are formed, increasing the system's surface area and contributing to additional energy barriers to pass.  Our data also indicate that the additional friction caused by textures originates from the adhesion between film surfaces rather than the viscosity of the film itself.  This interpretation is consistent with the results of an additional experiment where a mobile layer of foam was subjected to texture, and the increased friction experienced was attributed to the formation of edge contacts between the moving films.  This research uncovers the fundamental basis of texture-induced friction in complex liquids, demonstrating that it is a result of the interaction between the surface and the interior of the fluid, specifically the adhesion between film surfaces, rather than solely the interaction between surface and boundary, as is often assumed.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using image features and classification to identify abnormal skin cancer samples.

The interaction between a rapidly spinning outer liquid and a steady-flow inner liquid, which differs in density, was studied in a Hele-Shaw cell. The inner liquid's flow pattern was affected by the spin, even when it differed in density, we found. This density-neutral impact was seen in a hexagonal pattern of rotating interface instability, which the inner liquid's flow had to break through. The interface's stability was determined by the rate at which the inner liquid flows and the speed at which the outer liquid spins. The model was applied to predict the interplay between inner and outer liquids in a rapidly spinning container.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1-ethynyl-1-cyclopentadiene and 2-ethynyl-1-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. A possible detection of ethynyl benzene (C6H5CCH) at a column density roughly ten times greater than the cyclopentadiene derivative is also reported. The calculated abundances for ethynyl cyclopentadiene and ethynyl benzene are remarkably similar to that of cyano benzene (BCN), with ratios of 0.53±0.16 for the former in relation to the latter. The discovery of these ethynyl cyclical compounds may indicate they are formed through cyclic rearrangements of cyano and alkynyl compounds, or alternatively, share a common source with them.

In neural machine translation, the focus method selects specific neurons to limit the translation output based on input meanings, but it doesn't consider the importance of neurons in the output vocabulary. To address this, we propose a novel look-ahead focus method that weighs both the input and output neurons. During the decoding process, the proposed method first calculates the importance of each output neuron, then uses these weights to guide the attention mechanism. We evaluate the look-ahead focus method on four machine translation tasks: the results show that our method improves the metrics scores compared to the standard attention mechanism and the original focus method.

The significant progress achieved in grid computing was not merely the result of cumulative efforts, but also resulted from a collaborative project called Translating the Grid (TTG). Launched in 2001 by a group of researchers from Europe and the United States, TTG fostered an environment for interchanging ideas and developing common infrastructure. At its core, the project involved developing translations between different grid applications programming interfaces (APIs), which enabled users to utilize multiple APIs with a single interface, the Grid Application Programming Interface (GAPI). Although the results achieved during the project's duration were impressive, the fully realized potential of TTG remained unfulfilled due to limited documentation and inadequate continuation after the project's conclusion. Consequently, the project's contributions were largely overlooked in subsequent historical accounts. This paper aims to rectify this oversight by detailing the TTG approach, identifying key challenges, and exploring why the project's significant potential for grid computing was not fully realized.

A novel model, called the Dissipative Unified Dark Substance (DUDES) model, is presented for time that is dependent on distance, gravitational dynamics, particularly on the scales of cosmic evolution. The DUDES model combines two concepts, the dissipative gravity theory, which suggests that space-time has friction, and the unified dark matter-dark energy model, which proposes a single, undifferentiated dark component, with a different approach to addressing the Hubble tension. The model's parameters are determined through a fit to observational data, incorporating a range of cosmological observations, and it is evaluated how the model could be discriminated from existing dark matter and dark energy scenarios through electromagnetic signals from the early universe.

This study explores the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting a likelihood fit for various effective operators. This analysis led to strict bounds on light sterile neutrinos, specifically mass ranges below 195 MeV, and certain neutrino interaction cross-sections. Similarly, we established limits on the dark matter mass, ranging from 200 MeV to 1.6 GeV, and various cross-sections as J/ψ decay into invisible matter proves a sensitive probe of these phenomena.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

This research proves that for a random walk with reflection, whose step sizes have a probability density function, there is an infinite probability that the walk spends a fraction of time less than one step size within a certain distance from its starting point.

A plasma source called IShTAR has been developed for testing plasma interaction with magnetic fields in the International Stellarator Experiment (ISTE). To ensure successful operation, it's crucial to characterize its plasma accurately. Initial plasma scans revealed a non-uniform plasma distribution, which may indicate a missing component in the magnetic field. Further analysis showed that adding a missing magnetic field component, necessary for helical mode operation, could explain the observed results. Subsequent tests confirmed that IShTAR can operate in helical mode and produced plasma in the center of the device. Plasma characteristics measured during these tests included plasma density, temperature, and flux. To validate the results, additional tests were conducted with varying power and plasma density, which showed that plasma density decreased exponentially with increasing distance from the source. These findings were consistent with theoretical models, and multiple analysis techniques were used to validate the data, including checking for inconsistencies.

While gold-standard nuclear isolation for histopathology image analysis is considered the gold standard, it is often time-consuming and difficult to establish. As a result, there's a growing interest in automated solutions. Nucleus segmentation can serve as the basis for nuclear isolation, but current methods often suffer from over-segmentation characterizing dense areas, which negatively impacts detection of complex lesions. To address this issue, a novel W-Net architecture has been introduced, reducing dense area nucleic segmentation by exploiting the unique characteristics of dense areas. W-Net comprises two consecutive modules: a nucleus segmentation module followed by a density-based classification module to assign segmentation masks to samples. The architecture's design enables efficient training without relying on hand-crafted features. Experiments conducted demonstrate the efficacy of W-Net, outperforming established methods in tasks such as nucleus segmentation, density classification, and combined isolation, and revealing its potential for extending to tasks like cell-type segmentation and tumor tissue segmentation.

Let's consider a non-abelian group G that acts on a set X, and the group acts locally finitely on X. We develop the local exchange theorem for actions of certain Coxeter groups, specifically involving the special orthogonal group in odd dimension and the symplectic group in even dimension, with respect to a generating set defined by 2-letter relations. These results apply when the underlying field has a characteristic greater than 2 for the special orthogonal group and characteristically two for the symplectic group. The local exchange theorem enables us to determine the action of these Coxeter groups on X, by analyzing their action on the associated root system.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. The field's behavior can be reinterpreted using Chern-Simons form for a group of symmetries known as $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$, depending on specific parameters that either support $so(2,2)$, $so(3,1)$ or $iso(2,1)$ symmetries. The resulting equations of motion for this system are then depicted as non-linear partial differential equations. The soliton and black hole solutions are examined to determine their stability and temperature, with solitons found to be consistently cooler than black holes. The solution's stability is also tested under periodic perturbations, revealing that solitons are rigid and unshakeable, whereas black holes are unstable by spilling energy over time. The paper also delves into the interpretation of this theory using gauge fields, revealing that it resembles a standard Chern-Simons action, yet with a distinctive self-correcting feature. The possibility of this theory's applicability to certain phenomena, such as rotating hairy black holes and solitons, is finally considered.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Despite its advantages, the medical application of elastography is limited due to poor image quality resulting from inadequate tissue stabilization, overly aggressive strokes, or combination strokes involving both lateral and axial shifts. The key challenge in elastography is determining the lateral shift, as it is essential for differentiating soft tissues based on their mechanical characteristics but is prone to errors caused by the dominant axial shifting motion. This paper presents a novel approach, Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA), to accurately determine the lateral shift estimation in ultrasound elastography. VSSA involves dividing the appliance into individual source locations and synthesizing aperture images based on these sources to enhance axial resolution and determine the precise lateral shift. According to our results, VSSA significantly improves the accuracy of lateral shift estimation in elastography by reducing the error caused by Stokes' elastography by 81% in a simulation study involving regular sampling and 45% in an experimental study involving combined lateral and axial shifting motions.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning.

This problem has various applications, including reference trajectory creation for mobile robots and data classification, and it has been examined under different models, including static, dynamic, and distributed frameworks. This study concentrates on the dynamic $k$-centers problem, where cluster structures can evolve over time, and it offers a one-shot algorithm for approximating the optimal clustering configuration for a given set of points and target centers, with a desired dimension $d$ affecting the algorithm's performance. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games are first solved on a coarser state-level, and then the results are combined to determine the optimal action for the large-scale game. Each of these smaller games belongs to a subclass for which an exact optimal policy can be found through traditional means, such as value iteration. We connect these sub-games to the larger framework using transfer functions, which enable the efficient integration of different state-scales. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to a range of large-scale discrete stochastic evasion games.

While the number of vector bosons in the initial state is often a minor factor in proton-proton collisions, it will have a significant impact in future muon colliders, due to the similar masses of protons and muons. As a result, incorporating the full range of possible initial state vector bosons, rather than limiting it to only the fundamental electroweak bosons, becomes necessary for accurate and reliable calculations. The "vector boson approximation" refers to the practice of only considering the fundamental electroweak bosons in the initial state, which is typically valid in many applications of proton-proton collisions, but is no longer sufficient for muon colliders. In fact, studies have shown that neglecting additional initial state vector bosons can lead to errors in scattering crosssections of up to several percent, and even overestimation of crosssections by as much as 20%. To address this issue, a new method called the "efficient vector boson approximation" has been developed, which incorporates the effects of all possible initial state vector bosons while minimizing computational inefficiencies. This new method allows for accurate calculation of crosssections in the high-energy regime of muon colliders, both with and without the presence of initial state radiation. Furthermore, the efficient vector boson approximation serves as a foundation for more sophisticated approximations, and provides valuable insights into the behavior of crosssections in the high-energy limit.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to serious degradation when tasks are highly distinct.
We attribute this unfavorable outcome to catastrophic interference among the
tasks. To overcome this interference, we propose two approaches: changing the
way tasks are represented and using separate components of the model to reduce
sharing. Both strategies are effective in preventing the decline in performance
and help us identify that the problem lies in the ability to generalize, or
lack thereof, within the learned dynamics model. To validate these findings,
we conduct additional experiments showing that (1) there is an optimal balance
between task representation and generalization, and (2) the rate of learning
strongly impacts performance when tasks are similar. Ultimately, our study
shows that using a single dynamics model for multiple tasks is not necessarily
more beneficial than using separate models for each task, and that the way
tasks are represented significantly influences performance.
We explore an interesting development involving logics, specifically within the framework of intuitionistic modal logic, where we investigate the gathering of Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser.

We investigate the function $f\in NV$ within Clifford analysis, where $NV$ denotes the space of functions that are infinitely differentiable and non-vanishing. The aim is to explore the behavior of $f$ when it contains three distinct ball components, in relation to its transformation under the operator $\Delta$, which stems from the Dirac hypothesis. Through the analysis of the operator $\Delta$'s eigenfunctions in this context, we seek to establish the conjectured equivalence to the three balls conjecture, initially proposed by Sommers in 1978.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on minimizing the difference between the restored and true images, but also on selecting the most likely posterior distribution. Training models in this context is complex, especially when the measurement noise is substantial. We introduce a new regularized conditional GAN framework that directly learns the posterior distribution by reducing friction between the measured data and prior information. This is achieved by defining a new loss function that combines the diversity of generated images under the measurement noise distribution and prioritizes images that could plausibly arise from the true image when passed through an noise corruption process. This leads to a nonDifferentiable component in the loss function, so we use a sub-network to estimate the noise corruption process and facilitate model differentiability. We apply this framework to tasks like MRI with multiple coils and single coil output, showing its effectiveness in restoring realistic and diverse images.

This paper examines the existence of invariant surfaces in dynamical systems from a mathematical perspective. A novel approach is introduced to extend a longstanding theorem initially proved by Helmgolz, Kowalevski, Lie, and Sarazin. The implications of this approach for specific systems are also explored.

The interstellar medium is capable of revealing its complex structure and regional characteristics through the pattern of scintillation on pulsar images. By observing the Earth's passage through the medium using time-sensitive data and accurate positions, it is possible to identify specific phases of scintillation pattern variation. This study involves high-accuracy timing and position measurements for the pulsar PSR J1337+1600, which allows for a detailed examination of the interstellar medium on the path it takes during Earth's orbit. Furthermore, a comparison is made with the position of scintillation patterns varied over time, revealing regions of the interstellar medium that the Earth is passing through, specifically within the solar neighborhood. These regions correlate with the characteristics of the interstellar gas and plasma, as observed in the microwave spectrum, and can be found surrounding the cavity of the Sun, specifically surrounding the Local Bubble and the direction of the tangent point to the Earth's orbit, and also in the direction of the direction of the Sun towards the center of the galaxy.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through extended convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using an autoregressive structure and extensive convolutions. However, the lack of a clear relationship between the filter weights and the periodic nature of musical notes limits their effectiveness for tasks like pitch shifting. To overcome this constraint, the proposed QPNet incorporates three unique components: a pitch-dependent expanded convolution, a periodic residual module, and an adaptive dilation module. The pitch-dependent expanded convolution incorporates the spectral characteristics of waveforms at specific time frames to extend the convolution weights, thereby linking the periodic structure to the model. The proposed model demonstrates superior quality and stability compared to WaveNet and other baseline models for tasks like unconditional audio generation, pitch shifting, and song composition.

Bicategories serve as a base for the development of certain mathematical concepts, providing a framework that incorporates both symmetry and reversal. Within the realm of topological physics, bicategories can be used to model the relationships between spaces, incorporating both topological properties and mathematical markers known as topological invariants. Specifically, we can interpret the theory of shadows, a novel topological invariant recently discovered, in the context of bicategories. This connection reveals that shadows align with the principles of bicategories, demonstrating their comprehensive coverage. Consequently, we can define shadows using bicategorical methods and expand our understanding of them. Additionally, this approach provides a new perspective on the properties of shadows, shedding light on their intricate nature.

Deep neural networks depend on robust training data, and noisy inputs can significantly impede their performance. This research focuses on identifying the most challenging inputs in a dataset that can cause a deep neural network to fail, a problem we've termed "visual noise localization." To demonstrate the complexity of this issue, we've created a novel framework that incorporates optimal low-frequency image modulation and Gaussian noise in MNIST, resulting in a challenging dataset called NoiseIslands. Furthermore, we've established a clear understanding of the underlying challenges by analyzing the effects of noise and distortion in NoiseIslands. Our findings indicate that the difficulties with this dataset lie in its intermediate frequency range and that it shares similar characteristics with other complex image classification problems, such as face occlusion and adversarial attacks.

Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have been propelled by the massive amount of data being generated and the importance of scaling graph-based models. Unfortunately, many current GNN techniques rely on distant training, a process that requires substantial computational resources. A novel approach called Lorentzian GNN (LGNN) is introduced here to address this scalability issue. LGNN incorporates a unique non-linear activation function based on the Lorentzian formula, enabling faster learning and significantly reducing the need for distant training. Experimental results show that LGNN outperforms existing methods in multiple datasets across various tasks while requiring significantly less number of layers. In particular, LGNN achieves state-of-the-art performance on large-scale dataset CNM-1M, requiring a small fraction of layers compared to other methods.

This research focuses on identifying an object within a wave equation, specifically an internal source generating sound waves inside a closed container, using measurements from the container's exterior. A new inverse problem approach is introduced, and we prove its effectiveness by demonstrating the uniqueness of the object's composition and its position, and also establishing an error estimate for its numerical approximation.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context.

In this note, we explore a specific class of gravity theories, known as "hefty gravity", which are characterized by a unique symmetry between their metric and tensor components. We investigate harmonic gauge fixes for these theories and determine their fundamental metrics that satisfy the gauge conditions. We then examine the connection to general relativity and demonstrate that, in the context of hefty gravity, the harmonic gauge yields consistent results only when the gauge condition is applied in a modified manner. Additionally, we analyze the conformally hefty gravity category and provide an associated conformally flat gauge condition.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, thereby illustrating the underlying classical mathematical structure of this representation. This transformation exposes the symplectic matrix that defines the Poisson manifold of thermal parameters, thereby making the underlying geometry and topology of this manifold immediately apparent. We demonstrate this approach for several specific Hamiltonians, including the harmonic oscillator, both in its linear and nonlinear versions, as well as a Bose-glass system and a Bose-Einstein condensate subjected to decoherence. This method allows for the visualization of these states in phase space, making it an invaluable tool for studying the effects of temperature and disorder on these systems.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Within the easiest $s$-channel susy model, we examine the consistency of electroweak symmetry breaking and determine the parameter region that allows for the extrapolation of dark matter scattering cross-section off nucleons, while also assessing the reliability of Higgs vacuum stability predictions. To achieve this, we evaluate the phase space constraints imposed by recent experiments, including LHC $WW$ and $ZZ$ data, as well as the results from direct detection searches for dark matter. Our study indicates that, in order to maintain model validity, the ease criterion should be met through either intrinsic ease or intrinsic threshold ease, with calculations demonstrating that these conditions significantly shape the phase space. Furthermore, we find that recent findings from the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment essentially cover the parameters of the easiest scoto-seesaw model.

We use a one-band Hubbard model to investigate the orbitally degenerate $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ $Kramers$-doublet filled with $2.25$ electrons in 3D transition metal oxides. The model's results are compared to those of a lattice model, showing that the Hubbard model accurately captures the physical properties of this regime. The Blount parameterize the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ blending $Kramers$ doublets using four components, which are further reduced to three in some contexts. We demonstrate how the spread of $t_{2g}$ character among the $e_g$ sites, the coexistence of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ character among the $t_{2g}$ sites, and the spin-orthogonality of $t_{2g}$ sites can be extracted from the Hubbard model's Green's function. By numerically solving the model, we find that the spread of $t_{2g}$ character among the $e_g$ sites and the coexistence of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ character among the $t_{2g}$ sites decrease with increasing on-site Coulomb interaction, while the spin-orthogonality of $t_{2g}$ sites remains unchanged. This research focuses on the relative quantum geometric quantization in the context of algebraic geometry, specifically for symplectic reductions defined by ample line bundles. It is shown that for a certain class of birational transformations known as birational transformations keeping knot weights unchanged, the resulting reduced spaces yield equivalent relative quantum geometric quantizations. A concrete example involving the Fano surface embedded in projective space is also provided.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in medical imaging is being explored that involves incorporating realistic symptoms of lung conditions onto computed tomography scans of the abdomen. Current GAN-based techniques primarily focus on modifying head CT scans to simulate brain abnormalities, not considering the potential for overfitting due to limited available data. This novel application aims to demonstrate the potential of GAN-based editing for diagnostic purposes by incorporating authentic, large-scale data. In this study, realistic modifications were made to CT scans of the abdomen by incorporating authentic symptoms of lung conditions such as COVID-19, pulmonary embolism, and kidney disease. The edited images were created using a large dataset of chest X-rays with corresponding labels. The research further analyzes the potential for overfitting when using small datasets consisting of head and abdomen CT scans with associated pathologies. A solution to prevent overfitting is proposed by using a large dataset of chest X-rays. The results show that the generated images accurately reflect the incorporated lung conditions and can potentially aid in disease diagnosis. The research also explores the relationship between the extent of editing and the accuracy of the COVID-19 diagnosis using a large dataset of chest X-rays with corresponding labels.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool enables users to easily visualize high-dimensional data through embedding techniques such as PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, and others, and to interact with these visualizations in various ways. Additionally, ViDaExpert offers tools for clustering and classification visualization, and the application can be extended to accommodate custom methods via Java plug-ins.
